newsitem.title: USA: Coca Cola sees unit case volume, EPS on track.
newsitem.headline: Coca Cola sees unit case volume, EPS on track.

text.p: The Coca-Cola Co said on Tuesday the company was on track to meet its worldwide unit case volume growth of seven to eight percent for the full year.
The company said in a statement it also expected to meet its long term goal of earnings per share growth in the upper teens to 20 percent for the full year.

Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer James Chestnut was quoted as telling a meeting of financial analysts, "We expect to meet or slightly exceed the upper end of that volume growth target in 1996."
Chestnut also said Coca-Cola expected third quarter worldwide volume growth to increase six to seven percent and that earnings per share would meet consensus analyst estimates before unusual items.

The First Call mean estimate for the third quarter was $0.38 against $0.32 in the same period last year. The First Call mean estimate for fiscal 1996 was $1.39 against $1.19 for the same period last year.
The company said the combination of previously-announced unusual items was expected to have a net slight positive impact on its third quarter earnings.
Coca-Cola also said it was reducing concentrate inventory levels held by certain bottlers to strengthen its worldwide bottler system.
The reduction would result in a one-time $180 million to $200 million after-tax charge in the third quarter, it said.
Concentrate gallon sales in the quarter would be about even with sales in the same period last year, it said.

The company also said it would record a $60 million after-tax provision, for the launch of its "Project Infinity" plan. This was a strategic intiative to redesign the company's information systems and communications capabilities.
Coca-Cola also said it had taken various provisions totalling about $180 million to $200 million after-tax for structural changes at different divisions.
Structural changes would occur primarily in Greater Europe, Latin America and North America, mainly at Coca-Cola Foods, it said.

Adjustments ranged from a fundamental change in manufacturing and distribution process at Coca-Cola Foods, to streamlining operations in Germany, to closing a high fructose corn syrup production facility in Uruguay.
"The effect of these unusual items will be recorded throughout our third quarter income statement," Chestnut said.
